zone: Arrowhead Mountain — the Nason Creek roadside and the north ridge
_areas_note: One peak, its own file, and the honest headline is that ARROWHEAD HAS NO BACKCOUNTRY CAMP ON ITS ROUTE AT ALL. It is a 6,030 ft summit at the north end of the Chiwaukum Mountains, SOUTH of US 2 and south of Nason Creek, and it is climbed as a day outing — usually a winter one — from a highway pullout about seven miles east of Stevens Pass near the maintenance yard, at roughly 2,800 ft. The line walks the highway shoulder west, crosses the Nason Creek bridge, picks up an old logging spur and the railway grade, and climbs a steep wooded slope and a clearcut onto the north ridge, roughly six miles and three thousand feet round trip. There is no trail, no lake, no basin and no established site anywhere on it. NOT DUPLICATED from the Nason Ridge file, which removed this peak for exactly the right reason: Nason Ridge is the crest NORTH of the highway and its camps at Rock Lake, Crescent Lake, Merritt Lake and the lookout, together with the Nason Creek and Lake Wenatchee drive-in campgrounds, serve four summits Arrowhead has nothing to do with and cannot use. None of them appears below. Nothing is repeated from the Stevens Pass and Tye file either — Skyline Lake, Lichtenwasser, Lake Valhalla, Smithbrook and the Yodelin basin all sit on the far side of the highway or west of the pass. The peak's own file therefore consists of the roadhead, the one place on the mountain a party could bivouac, and the nearest drive-in ground that is not already written up elsewhere. SEASON IS THE THING TO GET RIGHT. This is a winter and shoulder-season objective by preference, not by accident: under snow the route is steep but avalanche-safe and the brush and clearcut slash are buried, while in summer the same ground is a slow thrash with no water and no reason to be there. Plan around snow cover rather than around the calendar.

sites.name: The US 2 pullout by the maintenance yard
sites.capacity: Shoulder parking and a pullout by the road turnoff for the maintenance station, with room for about three vehicles and space to sleep in one. There is no campground, no fee site, no table and no toilet. In winter the plough berm decides how much of it exists on any given morning.
sites.water: Nason Creek runs alongside and under the highway bridge the route crosses, and it needs treating. There is no potable supply. THERE IS NO WATER ON THE MOUNTAIN ITSELF once you leave the creek and the lower spur — the north ridge and the clearcut above carry nothing, so in summer everything is carried from here, and in winter the answer is melting snow.
sites.permit: None. This is not designated wilderness, there is no self-issue permit, no quota and no lottery anywhere on this peak. Highway shoulder parking needs no forest pass, which is worth knowing because the trailheads a few miles either side of it do. There is no fee and no registration. Note that the WSDOT rest area further along the highway is a rest area and not a campground, and overnight camping there is not what it is for.
sites.notes: This is the roadhead and, realistically, the accommodation. The pullout sits roughly seven miles east of Stevens Pass at the east tunnel end. The route walks west along the highway shoulder for a few hundred yards, crosses the Nason Creek bridge and drops onto an old logging spur that parallels the creek to the railway grade; parties then follow the tracks a short way before scrambling up the bank at about 2,700 ft and climbing steep timber to snowline around 3,700 ft. A variation stays on the spur, crosses Henry Creek, takes the right fork and then the left to the bottom of a clearcut at about 4,200 ft, climbs the clearcut directly south and traverses east into the trees to gain the north ridge. TWO CAUTIONS THAT ARE NOT ABOUT CLIMBING. The highway shoulder walk is on a fast, busy road with poor sightlines and is more dangerous than anything above it, and the railway line is active — treat both as hazards to be got off quickly rather than as part of the walk. Winter parking here is genuinely tight and the shoulder is where the ploughs put the snow, so an early arrival is worth more than an early start.

sites.name: The clearcut benches on the north ridge, around 4,200 feet
sites.capacity: No established site of any kind. Under deep snow the clearcut and the flat bench above it give as much room as a party wants; in bare conditions there is very little usable flat ground and it is all slash, stumps and brush. Recorded to say plainly that nobody camps on this mountain, rather than to invent a site for it.
sites.water: None whatsoever. Henry Creek on the lower spur is the last water on the way up and it is a long way below. In winter this is a snow camp and you melt; in summer you carry, and the amount you would have to carry is the argument against being here at all.
sites.permit: None — non-wilderness national forest and old logging ground, no permit, no quota, no fee. Fires are a poor idea in a clearcut full of dry slash and are prohibited under the summer restrictions that run most years on this side of the pass. Some of the lower spur network crosses a mix of ownership, so read the signs at the junctions rather than assuming everything is public.
sites.notes: Included as a contingency and as an honest negative. There is no reason to sleep on Arrowhead: the whole outing is six miles and three thousand feet and a fit party is up and down in seven or eight hours, so the only situation where this ground matters is a winter party that has broken trail through deep new snow, run out of daylight low down, and would rather bivouac than descend a steep wooded slope in the dark. Under those conditions the flat around the top of the clearcut at roughly 4,200 ft is the obvious place, being out of the timber and out of the terrain trap of the creek drainages. What you get is a snow camp with no shelter and no water; what you avoid is a night descent. In summer this same ground is slash and regrowth and there is nothing to recommend it. THE ROUTE IS CHOSEN FOR ITS AVALANCHE CHARACTER and is described as steep but safe by that measure, which is exactly the sort of judgement that changes with the year's snowpack — assess it rather than inheriting it.

sites.name: Tumwater Canyon campgrounds on US 2
sites.capacity: Small developed forest campgrounds strung along the highway in the canyon between Leavenworth and the Chiwaukum front, taking modest vehicles and a moderate number of parties. Sites are a mix of first come and reservable, and they fill on summer weekends with Leavenworth traffic that has nothing to do with the mountains.
sites.water: Piped potable water at the developed sites during the operating season, plus the river alongside. This is the one place in this file where water is not a problem, and it is the sensible place to fill everything before driving up to the pullout.
sites.permit: A per-night fee at the developed campgrounds, with some sites reservable in advance and the rest first come, first served. No wilderness permit is involved anywhere in this zone. Fire restrictions apply through the summer in the canyon and are commonly total bans by late season — this is one of the driest and most fire-prone stretches of highway in the state.
sites.notes: The nearest developed drive-in camping to Arrowhead that is not already recorded in a neighbouring zone file, deliberately chosen over the Lake Wenatchee corridor camps for that reason. It is a drive of half an hour or so west along the highway to the pullout, which suits a party that wants a proper night with water and a table before a dawn start. The catch is the season: these canyon campgrounds run roughly late spring to early autumn, which is precisely the half of the year when Arrowhead is at its worst. FOR THE WINTER ASCENT, WHICH IS THE ONE MOST PARTIES WANT, THESE ARE CLOSED and the answer is a night in the vehicle at the pullout or a very early drive from town. Note also that the December 2025 storms damaged forest roads across this district and a closure order covering them runs into 2027, and that a large fire closure sat over the Lake Wenatchee and Leavenworth country through the autumn of 2026; neither touches the highway itself, but both change what is open either side of it, so check before relying on a specific campground.

sites.name: The lower spur and Henry Creek flat
sites.capacity: Rough ground on the old logging road network in the first mile, where the spur crosses Henry Creek. Room for a tent or two on the road grade itself. Nothing established, nothing signed, and no reason to be here except timing.
sites.water: Henry Creek at the crossing, and Nason Creek below — both need treating and both run all year. This is the last water on the route and the only water on it, and its position at the very bottom of the climb is the whole water story of this peak: everything above is dry, so this is where you fill.
sites.permit: None. No wilderness, no permit, no quota. The spur network crosses mixed ownership in places, including railway and utility corridors, so read the signage at junctions and do not assume a road is open ground just because it is drivable-looking. No fee, no registration.
sites.notes: Recorded chiefly as the water point rather than as a camp, because knowing where Henry Creek is matters more on this mountain than knowing where you could pitch. The spur climbs east-southeast off the highway after the Nason Creek bridge, crosses the creek, and then forks twice — right at the first junction by an unnamed creek, left at the second — before reaching the bottom of the clearcut at about 4,200 ft. In winter the fork-finding is the navigational crux of the day and it is done under snow with the road cuts filled in, which is why parties who have been up before make much better time than parties who have not. As sleeping ground it is a poor substitute for the pullout, being no warmer, no flatter and a mile further from the car, and its one genuine use is for a party arriving in the small hours who would rather walk a mile and sleep than sit on the highway shoulder. Bring an axe for the steep timber above regardless of season; the slope from the railway grade to snowline is unrelenting.
